name: Text to SQL Benchmarks
title: Text to SQL Benchmarks
answer: Text to SQL benchmarks are test sets that measure how well a system turns a plain language question into a working SQL query. Public benchmarks such as Spider and BIRD score text to SQL systems by running the generated query and comparing its result with a known correct answer. They differ in difficulty, in how many tables and columns the questions touch, and in whether the questions are written for a single database or many. Enterprise schemas are larger and less tidy than the benchmarks, so real accuracy is usually lower. The benchmark result is a signal about a system, not a promise about how it will behave on a particular warehouse.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Running a benchmark means holding a database, a set of questions, and a set of reference queries or answers, then executing candidate queries against the database. The database engine does the heavy lifting, so the benchmark inherits its dialect, its data types, and its quirks. Evaluation harnesses execute each generated query, catch errors and timeouts, and compare the returned rows with the expected rows, often after normalising column order and formatting. Because execution is the scoring step, the environment has to be reproducible: the same schema, the same data, and the same engine version for every run. Larger models and hosted APIs are common, but the benchmark itself is mostly a database and a runner.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A typical evaluation takes a question and a schema description, asks a model to produce SQL, executes that SQL, and marks it correct if the result matches the reference. Matching is usually done on the result set rather than on the query text, because many different queries can be right. Some benchmarks also report exact match against a reference query, which is stricter and less forgiving of harmless differences. Systems are often given the schema, sample rows, or retrieved examples from similar questions, and the choice of what context to supply changes the score. Error analysis matters as much as the headline number, since a system can fail on joins, on ambiguous column names, or on questions the schema cannot answer at all.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Benchmark questions and reference queries come from somewhere, and their licence and provenance affect whether a system can be trained or tested on them. Some sets are built from public databases, others from contributed or synthetic schemas, and the terms differ. A high score on a public benchmark does not establish that a system is safe to point at production data, where permissions, row level security, and cost limits apply. Generated SQL can read more than intended, so execution is usually confined to a sandbox or a read only replica. Teams also need to record which model, prompt, and schema snapshot produced a score, because results drift when any of those change. None of this is legal advice, and the terms of a given dataset or model should be checked directly.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of the field is toward benchmarks that look more like real work: messier schemas, multi step questions, and evaluation on the actual database rather than a cleaned copy. There is growing interest in measuring whether a system knows when it cannot answer, and in scoring the cost and latency of a query alongside its correctness. Agent style systems that explore a schema, run a query, read the error, and try again are changing what a benchmark needs to capture. As models improve on the public sets, the useful signal shifts to held out and private evaluations that reflect a specific organisation's data. The benchmark remains a rough yardstick, and the gap between it and a given warehouse is where most of the practical work sits.
